turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the eighth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Today: America takes its blockade of Iran onto dry land, and a seafarer dies in the Gulf.
A nineteen forty-five Patek loses to a watch made in two thousand and two. [curious] By two point four million francs.
And Japan's calligraphy is recommended for the UNESCO list, on the way down.
On the way down?
Eight hundred and thirty thousand people stopped doing it in five years. Not yet in force. Almost everything today has been decided and not yet done.
That's a theme or that's an excuse.
It's a theme. You'll hear it four times before the sign-off.
Okay. Start me at the Gulf.
Saturday. United States Central Command announces a task force to cut off Iran's remaining overland and Caspian Sea shipments.
Overland. So the blockade leaves the water.
It leaves the water. Admiral Brad Cooper calls it a reinforcement of what he calls the ironclad blockade against Iran at sea.
And the strait itself?
Empty. The International Monetary Fund's shipping monitor logged one transit on the first of November. Against a baseline of eighty-five a day.
[exhales] That is not a chokepoint any more. That's a closed door.
Washington counts a hundred and forty-four vessels redirected through October, and about twenty-five billion dollars of Iranian crude sales prevented.
What's the human number? There's always a human number.
One. A crew member of the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire, killed on the fifth, in what's believed to be a missile strike.
[warmly] Name on the ship, no name on the man.
[thoughtful] Not published. Her Greek managers said the company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers.
And the rest of the week's damage?

This is the part I want you to hold onto. Iran's army claims three tankers struck mines. The Revolutionary Guard claims five vessels and a tug. Not one of those claims has been corroborated by any maritime authority.
So we don't know.
Worse. The United Kingdom's maritime trade operations centre says it is — their words — struggling to accurately report the count. Because ships have stopped reporting that they've been hit.
[pause] Right. If you report it, your insurance moves.
And your charter rate moves. So the register of what is happening in that strait is going dark while the strait itself is already dark.
Two views on the page today?

Doha and Beijing. Al Jazeera reads it as an American war of choice being talked down by Gulf mediators, and makes Washington's own vocabulary the evidence. Trump called Friday's raids minor strikes. Qatar's prime minister, at Oxford, says the crisis cannot be left unresolved. Global Times runs a professor from Shanghai saying China's intensive mediation provides an important international public good. By a country that, he writes, does not seek spheres of influence.
Does the piece mention America? [laughs] That's the whole op-ed, then. Who's the sceptic?

Fereidun Fesharaki, of the consultancy FGE, to Bloomberg on Thursday: not only are we not close to a resolution, we are even worse than we were before the June memorandum. He thinks Tehran reads the midterm result as a weakened president. And he puts what's left of Iran's exports at two to three hundred thousand barrels a day, overland, through Iraq.
Which is exactly what Saturday's task force is for.
Which is exactly what Saturday's task force is for.
Money. What happened to the ten-year?
It fell five basis points. Four point eight six per cent on Friday.
Good. Bonds doing their job while stocks fall. No?
The same bond stripped of inflation went the other way. The real ten-year rose a basis point, to two point six three.
[curious] Okay, explain that to me like I'm holding the thing.
A bond's yield is what you expect inflation to be, plus what you want to earn on top. If the first falls and the second rises, nothing has improved. Something just got cheaper.
And the something is?

Oil. Brent went from a hundred and seventeen dollars to ninety-eight in a week. More than. So the entire rally in that bond was the market marking down expected inflation because the war premium came out of crude. Not growth. Not rescue.
So the hedge didn't hedge.

A global all-world equity holding fell one point eight nine per cent on the week. A global aggregate bond proxy rose nought point six nine. Right sign, wrong size. The bond leg offset under a sixth of the drawdown. Held in October. Two dissents — both wanting a rise.
Both for a hike. [pause] That's not the story I've been reading anywhere else.

Futures put about seventy-three per cent on an increase on the ninth of December. And zero on a cut. Zero. The European Central Bank raised in September. The Bank of Japan has a dissenter who wants one and a half per cent. Three central banks leaning tighter into a growth scare.
What actually diversified, then?
Gold. Up four and a half per cent on the week — against both of its textbook drivers.
Meaning real yields up, dollar flat, and it rose anyway.

Central banks bought three hundred and twenty-one tonnes in the third quarter, up forty-two per cent, while total demand fell. Behaved like a leveraged risk asset. About thirty per cent below its high for the year while gold sits near its own. Explanation, not advice. Both of them.
Home. Two data breaches here?

M one and Doctor Anywhere. Both told customers on Friday evening. Neither said how many people are affected. Neither. M one lists names, identity-card numbers, dates of birth, mobile numbers, email and home addresses.
[sighs] The identity-card number is the one that matters.
You can reset a password in a minute. You get one of those numbers for life.
What's on offer? Credit monitoring, anything?

Notification, and a request to remain vigilant. Alfred Siew at Techgoondu wrote the line of the week on it. This isn't good enough. Investigating M one. But here's the sceptic's point, and it's a good one: an unpublished number is an unprovable harm.
Because the penalty is proportionate to the scale —

— and nobody has stated the scale. Meanwhile the biggest recent leak here, seventy thousand people at the Land Authority, drew no fine at all. Government agency. Not fineable under the Act. One more. The seven hundred million dollars restrained in the Prince Holding Group case — the woman arrested at Changi was charged with two counts. Both about one document submitted to a lease application in twenty twenty-two.
Neither of them a money-laundering charge.
Neither. Restraint is not forfeiture. Nothing has been confiscated.
Not yet in force. Twice now. Technology. The chip rout — was that really about regulation?

Start with the fact nobody reported. On the third of November, voters in ten American states decided forty-one local ballot questions about data centres. Forty of them went against the industry. Five outright bans. Twenty-one of the forty-one were in Ohio alone.
[gasps] Forty out of forty-one. That's not a swing, that's a verdict.
Two days later the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell twelve and a quarter per cent. Its worst day since March of twenty twenty.
So regulation did it.

Maybe not. Look at who fell hardest. Micron down seventeen and a half. AMD down seventeen. Nvidia — the most exposed name there is — down nine. Backwards for a regulation story. That's the shape of a capital-spending scare. And Barclays' credit strategist says the pushback is bipartisan but local, which makes the buildout pricier rather than stalling it. Five to eight per cent on Friday, with no policy change at all.
Meanwhile AMD had its best quarter ever.

Thirteen point four billion dollars, up forty-five per cent, and it fell seventeen anyway. One more, for the home lab. Samsung will charge four dollars ninety-nine a month to let Home Assistant talk to your own appliances.
Wait — appliances I already own?
Appliances you already own. From the fifteenth of December the current connection stops working. In every country. The plan is only sold in some of them.
[scoffs] That's the bit. Somebody in Jakarta loses their fridge dashboard and can't pay to get it back.
A man on their own forum called it a horribly regressive step. And another made the point that people running Home Assistant are not developers, they're end users.
Is there a defence?
There is, and it's honest. The charge sits on the cloud. Local drivers, Matter devices, all still free. So the lesson is buy Matter, not cloud appliances.
Unless it's a fridge.
Unless it's a fridge. Those speak nothing else.
The Kit — quickly, because I know what you're going to say about it.
Laowa put the first f-two tilt-shift lens on sale. Twelve hundred and forty-nine US dollars.
Tilt-shift is the one that keeps buildings from leaning.

That, and it swings the plane of focus. They've never been fast. This one covers medium format. Nobody has measured it. Every image in circulation is the maker's own. The fastest tilt-shift yet is their sentence, not a test result.
[laughs] So we're reporting a specification.
We're reporting a specification and saying so.
And the Atelier today?

Pressure cookers. And the thesis is one line: the valve is the entire product. Food can't get hotter than the water it sits in. Seal the pot, raise the pressure, the boiling point climbs. Reaction rates roughly double every ten degrees.
So a recipe written for one pot can just be wrong in another.

Exactly right. Which is why this is the number that got me: Fissler publishes three operating temperatures. Hawkins publishes none. Prestige publishes none. Not in the catalogue, not in the price list. And America's Test Kitchen put eight of them on instruments last November — only one reached two hundred and fifty degrees.
And the buy-once test?
Kuhn Rikon sells two complete valve assemblies. One for cookers made before nineteen ninety-eight, one for after.
[warmly] Oh, that's lovely. They'll still fix a pot you bought in ninety-seven.
That's the whole desk in one part number.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole. What have we got?

Shodō. Japanese brush calligraphy. And it has a news peg three days old: on Wednesday, Japan's culture agency announced that UNESCO's evaluation body has recommended inscribing it. The committee decides in Xiamen, between the first and the third of December.
Xiamen. In China.
In China. Chinese calligraphy was inscribed in two thousand and nine.
[laughs] So Japan is seventeen years behind the parent tradition, and will hear the verdict in the parent's living room. Why does Japan even need the listing? Everyone there does this at school.
They do, and it's by ministerial order. Brush writing in every year from the third grade of primary, about thirty timetabled hours a year, then twenty, twenty and ten in lower secondary.
Add it up for me.
Roughly a hundred and seventy hours of brush calligraphy for every child in Japan.
[gasps] A hundred and seventy. That's a university course.
And since the twenty seventeen revision, the first two grades practise with water brushes. The marks evaporate as they dry.
[drawn out] That is the most Japanese sentence you've said all week.
And yet the adults are leaving. The government's own time-use survey: four point one per cent practised in twenty sixteen, three point four in twenty twenty-one.
How many people is that?
About eight hundred and thirty thousand fewer in five years. A real one. The later survey was taken in October of twenty twenty-one. Inside the pandemic.
Fair. Now do the gear, because that's why I'm here.
Four things. A brush, an ink stick, a stone to grind it on, and paper.
And the whole functional kit costs?

About a hundred and fifty Singapore dollars. That's it. Everything above that buys craft, not performance. But the craft is extraordinary. Kumano, in Hiroshima, publishes the twelve principal steps of making a brush — tradition counts seventy-three.
What's the step people never hear about?

The hair is mixed with rice-husk ash and pressed with a hot iron. To kill the curl, and draw the oils out. Hair with oil in it won't take up ink at all. Then the bundle is tapped on a plate so the tips migrate to one end. Bad hairs are picked out by feel, with a small knife. By feel. Then a thin skin of better hair is wrapped around the cheaper core — so what you see hides what you paid less for — and the whole thing is heat-set, which fuses the proteins and locks the shape.
And the scale of that town?
Twenty-four million brushes a year. About nine point six billion yen. Two thousand people, a tenth of the town.
How many hold the national craft title? [pause] Eleven. Out of two thousand.
And here's the one that stopped me. There is now one company left in Japan making pine soot.
One. For the ink.
[thoughtful] For the ink.
What's the money pit?
Old ink and Chinese stone. Nearly three hundred thousand yen for a stick of mid-nineteenth-century soot. About a million for a good Chinese inkstone.
And does it write better?
Nobody can tell you. There is no published blind comparison of any of it.
What do the makers say?
This is my favourite thing in the issue. On their own cooperative's website, the Kumano brush makers write that a good brush is one that suits your purpose, not necessarily the most expensive one.
[laughs] The sellers are talking you down.
And they call brushes consumables. Meanwhile the same shape from a named Nara artisan is forty to fifty-five thousand yen against one to six thousand from the examination association's shop.
Twelve to seventeen times.
On an object its own trade body calls disposable.
And the ranks? There's always a ladder.
Two systems. The examination is clean — ministry-endorsed, published criteria, thirty-one thousand five hundred yen for all eight brush levels.
And the catch?
Time. It runs once a year. Eight grades, eight years, and no money shortens it.
And the other system?

Exhibitions and prizes. Fifteen thousand yen to enter one work. And when a judging scandal at Japan's most prestigious art exhibition was examined by a third-party committee, the committee's findings about the calligraphy section used two phrases. Rule by elders. And a money-driven constitution.
[exhales] And the organisation's response?
Declined most of the questions as unsuitable for it to answer. Said it endeavours to ensure fairness.
So the honest advice is skip the second system entirely.

Buy the hundred-and-fifty-dollar kit. Lurk. And if you want one upgrade, make it the stone — because you can feel the difference on the first stroke. Godzilla Minus Zero took fourteen and a half million US dollars in North America on Friday, its first day.
And at home?

It opened in Japan on Culture Day and took nine hundred and ten million yen in a single day. The highest opening day any live-action film has ever had there. The weekend isn't finished. So we don't print one. There's a dissent, too, and it's Japanese. Toyo Keizai ran a piece headlined — you don't need to watch the last five minutes. The reaction at home has split over the ending. The Journe beat the Patek. A platinum Chronomètre à Résonance from two thousand and two made eight point six eight million francs.
And the nineteen forty-five steel Patek everyone came for?
Six point two seven million. Which was fifty-seven per cent above its own top estimate, and still second.
A living maker outbids a dead one. [thoughtful] That's a shift.

And the body. A Faroese trial — fourteen weeks of small-sided football, a hundred and eleven adults aged forty to seventy. It missed its own primary target. No lean mass at all. And peak oxygen uptake rose substantially anyway.
Why do we like that study?
Because they said in advance what they were looking for, didn't find it, and published it that way.
What's the transferable bit?
Weeks one and two were walking football. Normal play only from week three.
[warmly] That's the on-ramp. That's how a forty-something doesn't tear something.
General guidance, not medical advice.
And the travel desk — give me one.

Japan took the red-crowned crane off its Red List in March. Mostly. Hokkaido's own census counted nineteen hundred and two birds in January — flat on the year. But the number of places they were recorded in went from two hundred and sixty-nine to three hundred and ninety-two.
In one winter?
In one winter. The artificial feeding that concentrated them is being dispersed, deliberately, on disease grounds.
[thoughtful] So the photograph everybody goes for is being switched off.
Over years, not months. But yes. Go soon, or go for something else.
And the long read?

India. And it's the best thing in the book. In a Bengaluru courtroom in July, a judge looked at six of the largest technology companies in India, all suing the state of Karnataka, and asked why they were litigating over a levy of fifty paise.
Fifty paise. That's — what, a Singapore cent?
[curious] About. It's the welfare fee a platform pays each time it pays a rider for delivering food.
And they hired senior counsel to fight a cent. So it isn't about the cent.

It is not. India has quietly stopped asking whether the gig worker is an employee. The answer, never announced, is no. Permanently. A price. One per cent of each payout, capped in paise. Fifty for a two-wheeler delivery, a rupee for a car.
Read the cap for me.
That's the trick. One per cent capped at fifty paise binds on anything above fifty rupees. On a five-hundred-rupee cab fare the effective rate is nought point two per cent.
So the headline rate is theatre and the cap is the policy.

And the collection proves it. For the April-to-June quarter, six named platforms deposited about four crore rupees. The state projected two hundred and fifty to three hundred crore a year. Fifty-seven rupees a quarter. About a rupee a week.
[deadpan] That buys nothing.
It was never going to. And in March, Zomato raised its own platform fee by two rupees forty — nearly five times the maximum welfare fee on a delivery.
So what are they actually fighting about?

Section twenty-one. Karnataka's law creates a payment and welfare fee verification system. Telangana's creates its twin, and the Telangana wording is the one to read: all payments to platform workers mapped onto a government system, on a real-time basis.
[drawn out] Oh. It's a meter.
It's a meter. The first live, transaction-level register of informal income in a large economy. Not a survey. A feed.
And the fifty paise is the installation fee.
That's the sentence. And one board member let it slip — he said the companies had been reluctant to share real-time data.
Where's the Centre in this?

Here's the part that gives it away. The Union government wrote its own levy on turnover, back in twenty twenty. Six years later the rate has never been notified. As of the eighteenth of October, nothing in the gazette. So five states built a meter instead. And when Karnataka was challenged in court, the Union government's own law officer appeared for the companies.
Against its own state.
Arguing the state had trespassed on its field.
[exhales] That's not a government protecting workers.
That's a government defending a tax base it hasn't learned to collect.
Is there a precedent?

An exact one. Nineteen ninety-six, a cess on construction, the same one-to-two per cent band. Thirty years on: one point one three lakh crore collected, about sixty-eight thousand crore spent, and nearly sixty-three thousand crore sitting unspent.
Against how many workers?
Five point seven three crore registered.
So the money doesn't move.
And the paper written for the labour ministry asks for a data hub, dashboards, a digital passbook. Which is precisely what the gig laws already have inside them.
The old cess, rebuilt with the data layer.
The argument, in one line: India is not insuring its gig workers. It is metering them, and the price of the meter is fifty paise an order.
[pause] And the counter?

Fair and real. Nothing collected at scale, nothing paid out, and the whole state version could be struck down. The eligibility gate alone is ninety days with one platform, when disclosures suggest the average rider works under forty days a year.
A levy on everyone, funding benefits for almost nobody.
And three of the big platforms have resigned from the Karnataka board rather than sit under a law they're challenging.
[thoughtful] So the honest version is: the mechanism is real, the magnitude isn't. Yet.
Not yet in force. Fourth time.
[laughs] You did say.
The question to carry out of it isn't whether fifty paise is enough. It's what a government does with a live feed of fifty million people's earnings once it has one.
And whether anyone asked before the tap went in. [warmly] That's the book.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
